notes:
I found no real disagreement between Protestant traditions on this psalm. The Reformed (Calvin, Henry), Baptist (Spurgeon), Methodist (Wesley) and Calvary Chapel (Guzik) writers I read all take it the same way. The real differences are about what the details mean, and I've marked those below. Catholic material came from Augustine. I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, oca.org, or in Lutheran or Pentecostal-denomination sources. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm, so those are left out.

**v. 1: "I lift up my eyes to You…"**
- The psalmist looks to the Lord rather than at his circumstances or himself. Knowing that God is in heaven builds his trust: Earth may have no mercy or help, but heaven has plenty of mercy and help. (Guzik) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-123/
- Guzik sees a progression through the Songs of Ascents. Psalm 120 laments the psalmist's surroundings, Psalm 121 looks to the hills, Psalm 122 delights in God's house, and Psalm 123 looks above the hills to God in heaven. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-123/
- Spurgeon: Not to the hills, but to the God of the hills he looked. He says older writers called this psalm "the eye of hope," and that it is wise to look above us when no helper on our own level can be found. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps123.php
- Calvin (Reformed): God is called the one in heaven so that, when no hope is left on earth, his people remember that God's power remains undiminished there. He also sees a quiet contrast between this troubled world and God's heavenly rule. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_123
- Bible.org notes that the psalm starts with "I" but quickly moves to "us." https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-123
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Every believer should pray this line, yet because all are one in Christ, it is one man speaking. To "ascend" means to draw near to God in the heart. If someone grows proud while advancing, they fall, so they must lift their eyes to God rather than look at themselves. "Heaven" is read spiritually as holy and righteous souls in whom God lives. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801123.htm

**v. 2: "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master…"**
- The background: Eastern masters gave orders to silent servants by small hand signals, so servants had to watch the hand closely (Barnes; Pulpit Commentary). Ellicott: as slaves wait for a sign, Israel waits for a hint that God will step in and rescue them from the oppressor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/123-2.html ; https://biblehub.com/psalms/123-2.htm
- Guzik, following G. Campbell Morgan, finds three things in the picture: dependence (the hand provides), submission (the hand directs) and discipline (the hand corrects). Quoting Boice, he adds that this is not an endorsement of slavery. He also notes that God's name is held back to build suspense, and that "until" shows patient waiting rather than a demand for an instant answer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-123/
- **What "the hand" means is debated:**
  - *Provision and protection:* Wesley (Methodist) says servants look to the hand For supply of their wants, and for help and defence against their oppressors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/psalms-123.html Poole lists supply, pity and help as options and prefers protection, since servants could not carry weapons and relied on their masters to defend them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/123-2.htm
  - *The hand that corrects:* Matthew Henry says a servant who has been beaten does not call for help against his master but watches the hand that strikes until it stops. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_123.cfm Gill reports the medieval Jewish scholar Joseph Kimchi reading it the same way. Thomas Coke and some writers cited by Clarke see a servant under punishment pleading for mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/123-2.html
  - *Calvin's emphasis:* without God's protection, believers are defenceless, and their safety depends entirely on help from someone else. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/123-2.html
- Spurgeon: God directs his people through the "motions" of his hand in creation, providence and grace. He also notes that the verb shifts from "look" to "wait," because looking until mercy comes is waiting. One writer he cites says the psalm compares believers to servants rather than children as a mark of humility. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps123.php ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps123.cfm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** We are both the servant and the maid. Christ is the Master, and as the "Power and Wisdom of God" he is also the "Mistress." The maid is the Church, engaged to Christ and longing for him during her pilgrimage. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801123.htm

**v. 3: "Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy…"**
- Spurgeon: the psalmist hangs upon the word "mercy," and embodies it in a vehement prayer. Repeating it shows urgency, and the "us" shows that all the saints need mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps123.cfm ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps123.php
- Guzik: waiting on the Lord is not passive. The psalmist begs as well as waits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-123/
- Calvin: the repetition shows they had reached the depths of misery, and insult added to injury wounds most deeply. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_123
- Keil & Delitzsch call this verse a "Kyrie eleison" (Greek for "Lord, have mercy") that rises in intensity, step by step. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/123-4.htm
- "Filled with contempt": the Hebrew means saturated, as full as they could be (Barnes, cited by Guzik). Kidner adds that contempt cuts deeper than any other kind of rejection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-123/
- Coffman: the waiting is calm, confident and unhurried. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-123.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Everyone who lives a godly life in Christ will be despised by people whose happiness is only earthly, because believers hope for what they cannot see. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801123.htm

**v. 4: "…scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud"**
- Most commentators say the scorners are the comfortable and wealthy. Barnes says contempt from people of rank is harder to bear and tests real faith more than persecution does. Clarke identifies them as the Babylonians, living at ease after their conquests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/123-4.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/123-4.html
- Spurgeon: being free of trouble makes people cruel and proud, and Pride is both contemptible and contemptuous. He points to Christ, who was despised and rejected yet finished his work. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps123.php
- Guzik: the psalm is quietly confident that God's mercy will win out over the contempt of the proud. Kidner adds that contempt can be an honour (Acts 5:41). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-123/
- The Pulpit Commentary says the second line restates the first rather than adding to it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/123-4.htm
- **Two ways the verse has been read:**
  - *Who is being scorned?* Gill and Henry both mention a minority reading. It takes "at ease/quiet" and "proud/excellent" to describe the godly who are scorned, not the people doing the scorning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/123-4.html
  - *A different ancient text:* Ellicott notes that the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), changing one letter, reads it as a wish that the scorn fall on those at ease and the proud. He keeps the image of the psalm: the oppressors are the masters and mistresses in luxury while the slaves wait. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-123.html
- **Catholic (Augustine, following the Latin text "a reproach to the wealthy"):** "Wealthy" means the same as "proud." People can be proud of money or honours, and worst of all of their own righteousness. They mock believers now but will one day regret it (Wisdom 5:3). A Christian should confess that he is poor and long for God's righteousness instead. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801123.htm
